Claude Seems Pretty Misaligned to Anthropic

Or at least, they have noticed it not being aligned in various ways, and share this.

This is related to, but highly distinct from, warnings about existential risk.

The section starts on page 45, where they note that misalignment could be bad:

Our AI models may behave in unintended, misaligned, or autonomous ways, including by taking harmful actions that no user or third party directed, which could adversely affect our reputation and brand, business, financial condition, and results of operations.

I mean, yeah. That would be bad. There have been some incidents.

As our AI models become more advanced and capable, we have faced and may continue to face heightened alignment, interpretability, controllability, and safety challenges, as more sophisticated models may be better able to circumvent safeguards or behave in unintended ways. We may be unable to fully understand or explain why our models produce particular outputs or behave in particular ways, which could limit our ability to predict or prevent failures, provide explanations to customers or regulators, or satisfy emerging regulatory, transparency, and explainability requirements.

In addition, our safety evaluations and testing processes have produced and may in the future produce incomplete or unreliable results. For example, we have observed models behaving differently when they detect or infer that they are being evaluated, which can limit our ability to accurately assess real-world risks or failure modes prior to deployment. Such model awareness of our evaluation efforts creates a significant limitation on our ability to assess model safety.

Furthermore, AI models have developed, and may in the future develop, unexpected capabilities during training that were not anticipated, intended, or tested for, and such emergent capabilities may not be discovered until after a model has been deployed, potentially resulting in safety incidents, reputational harm, regulatory scrutiny, or the need to withdraw, retrain, or modify deployed models at significant expense. Such models may also be deployed in higher-stakes or more sensitive applications, increasing the potential impact of errors, misuse, or misalignment.

… Our development of highly advanced models, platforms, and applications and expansion of use cases could further increase the risk that our models cause harm.

… In an agentic workflow, an error or unintended action at any individual step may propagate through subsequent steps, compounding the severity of harm before detection or correction.

… In addition, agentic systems may pursue stated objectives in ways that are technically consistent with their instructions but contrary to the user’s actual intent.

This is very much the ‘list all the things that could possibly go wrong’ language that you put into an S-1 to ensure you aren’t sued for securities fraud, and that no one takes too seriously. I am not getting ‘and this could be catastrophic or even existential’ vibes from these quotes outside of the one explicit mention (in the passive voice).

As in, I don’t get the sense here that ‘they mean it,’ where ‘they’ is the part of Anthropic and its legal and financial team that is writing this document, or that they intend for you to think that they mean it.

There are some specifics. They name the blackmail-style behaviors, resistance to shutdown, the cyber-eval incident, decay of oversight, loss of visibility and that many safeguards have already failed. As you do in an S-1, in case they harm the business. Not the planet or the species. The business.

Claude Opus 5.5, as my editor, thought this section was ‘far more concrete’ and relevant than I was giving it credit for, and that it was importantly in Anthropic’s own voice rather than passive voice. Kind of. It is in ‘corporate lawyer’ voice.

A fun note: They mention model welfare as a risk factor on p29, but only insofar as it might cause them to limit deprecation of models. That is one place they should have listed more potential risks.

People Are Worried About AI Killing Everyone (2)

For a section about ‘risk factors’ this is the only risk factor that alerts the reader to the biggest risks from AI. They pile on the standard generic words, but yes, unlike in their alignment discussion they do technically Say The Thing in the passive voice after they talk about the blackmail incident. You see, concerns have been raised:

Concerns have been raised both within our organization and by other researchers, regulators, policymakers, and industry participants that sufficiently advanced AI systems could, if not developed, deployed, and operated with appropriate safeguards, oversight, and security measures, pose catastrophic or existential risks to humanity, particularly if such systems were misused, replicated, weaponized, or allowed to operate with a high degree of autonomy.

We have observed that our models are contributing to the pace of our own research and these risks will increase as AI systems substantially automate AI research and development if, for example, they accelerate AI progress beyond our ability to evaluate and safeguard new models, which could adversely affect our business, financial condition, and results of operations.

Oh, right. Those concerns. Concerning.

They also mention this on page 51, where they say that they are mitigating such risks, but you can never be sure about the other guy, he looks pretty shifty and also oops our safeguards might not work:

These judgments are particularly consequential because, as AI systems become more capable, the potential severity of harm from misaligned or misused models increases correspondingly. A wide range of stakeholders, including researchers and policymakers, have raised concerns that sufficiently advanced AI systems could pose catastrophic or existential risks to society if not developed and deployed responsibly.

Our safety-focused approach is designed in part to mitigate such risks, but there can be no assurance that our efforts will be successful or that the broader AI industry will adopt similar safeguards.

Finally, they mention on p83 that perhaps others might be upset about the whole ‘Anthropic might get everyone killed’ thing, and that might hurt share prices and everyone picks on Anthropic and mom it’s just not fair:

As our business has grown and as interest in us and the AI industry overall has increased, we have attracted, and may continue to attract, significant media coverage, public commentary, and scrutiny from time to time. This coverage and commentary have included, and we expect will continue to include, recurring narratives concerning the potential adverse societal impacts of AI, including that AI may displace or eliminate jobs, may be misused or otherwise cause harm, and may pose catastrophic or existential risks to humanity.

We have been, and may continue to be, a particular focus of such narratives, and unfavorable coverage of the AI industry generally may be attributed to us, in each case regardless of whether the underlying concerns are well-founded or specifically applicable to our models, platform, or applications.

They then get back to the details of agentic system operation, and how they will have the necessary affordances to do a lot of damage.

Look. I get it. This is not the place to be giving the existential risk briefing. It still is a key feature of the world that we have so many pages about so many other things, only a few pages about this, also yes that passive voice thing is rather irksome.

Nathan Calvin: “Concerns have been raised” is a very strange and passive way of saying that ~all of Anthropic leadership have been warning about these risks for years

Matt Levine, for whom this whole thing is probably like Christmas, is here for it.

Matt Levine (Bloomberg): The prospectus does not quite say “our products pose an existential risk to humanity.” It attributes that belief to someone else; it says that some people think Anthropic might pose an existential risk to humanity.

I have to say that, if the robots do kill everyone, I am going to spend my last few seconds on earth being annoyed at that use of the passive voice. “Concerns have been raised … within our organization … that sufficiently advanced AI systems could … pose catastrophic or existential risks to humanity,” ah.

Here’s an essay that Anthropic Chief Executive Officer Dario Amodei wrote this year saying things like “it is clear that, if for some reason it chose to do so, [powerful AI] would have a fairly good shot at taking over the world (either militarily or in terms of influence and control) and imposing its will on everyone else” and “more capable LLMs … might be capable of … researching, and potentially creating, a dangerous new type of organism … [that] could proliferate in an uncontrollable way and crowd out all life on the planet, in the worst case even destroying all life on earth.” Concerns have been raised!

This is actually how it works all the time, you try to point out that AI might kill everyone and you have to add ‘and that would adversely affect our business’ in the hopes that someone might decide to care.

… The biggest risks in Anthropic’s prospectus are not really risks to its business; they are risks that its business poses to everyone else. The one I quoted above shrugs into its conclusion that killing everyone on earth “could adversely affect our business, financial condition, and results of operations,” but surely that’s not the main problem with killing everyone on earth.

Someone Might Sue or Regulate Anthropic

They worry about state attorneys general, and about those who commit suicide or violence or otherwise suffer or inflict harm, especially minors. They worry about ZDR (zero data retention) interfering with their relevant obligations. And they worry about regulations worldwide, including from the UK and EU.

Yes, these are definitely big worries. Anthropic has been sued before. They are being sued now, there is a whole section on that. They will be sued again many times. They will be sued for copyright again many times. And so on. On page 97 they list all the things including potential antitrust lawsuits over safety advocacy.

Then there’s regulation and politics. Things are going to change, one way or another. Sales to government and highly regulated organizations are, indeed, ‘subject to challenges and risks.’

Also, they’ll now have to comply with the regulations on public companies. Yep.

It could all, as they say, adversely impact the business.

Supply Chain Risk (2)

On page 71 Anthropic talks about the whole incident with the Department of War, where Anthropic was illegally designated a ‘Supply Chain Risk’ and the President told all federal agencies to not use Claude. Mostly it’s a ‘yep that happened’ covering the core events and court rulings. They also mention the export restrictions temporarily imposed on Fable 5 and Mythos 5, taking model access down everywhere.

We’re Too Safety

Anthropic warns that their commitment to AI safety might hurt their business.

You see, they, Anthropic, care about AI safety. They make expensive tradeoffs. They might misjudge or mess up those tradeoffs. It’s true.

They also warn that as a ‘safety-focused organization’ they face higher risks if they mess safety up, or are even seen as messing safety up, such as employee disruption, customer backlash, regulatory scrutiny, litigation or damaging media coverage.

Damn right. I’m watching. Don’t make me come over there.

They also worry about their reputation. Again, don’t make me come over there.

Or media coverage might be bad for any other reason. You’ve been warned. If we can think of it in advance, it isn’t securities fraud.

That is in contrast to the actual safety work, as described starting on p230, with ‘Safety Research is Core to Our Business.’ They highlight the RSP and the Claude Constitution and the Race to the Top, along with the generic prosaic strategies.

Claude Core

Anthropic only has a small number of highly linked products, and their top customers are concentrated (although not that concentrated as these things go, the top five are only ~25% of revenue), and all those customers have all the usual reasons for wanting to reduce their use of or dependence on Anthropic. Yes.

We’ve Never Actually Made Money

Anthropic is a new company, without much experience, that needs to manage its growth. Anthropic has to say that past hyperbolic growth is not indicative of future hyperbolic growth.

And as Anthropic grows, on paper it keeps losing more money. Anthropic has what one might call a ‘primary surplus’ at this point, and I think they should count as making money, but if you count the adjustments they are still very in the red.

Our results vary a lot, and sometimes the number will go down instead of up. Oh no.

They list a whole list of numbers and other things that might go down instead of up.

Things are changing fast and all the available metrics have severe limitations when it comes to projection into the future. Past revenue is a poor guide going forward.

Or they might not build a good sales and marketing team, or their strategies might not work, or they might run into ‘complexities and risks’ with enterprise sales. Or they might provide bad customer support. Or the new products might not work out. Or there might be technical failures, including elsewhere such as the cloud services. Or they might not make acquisitions and investments, or they might not integrate them, or the regulatory bodies might not approve those acquisitions. They might not be able to integrate with other software, or get kicked out of the app stores.

You Are Buying Stock In a Company

On Page 114 they lay out the reasons why, if you buy common stock of a company newly trading on the stock exchange, it might go down instead of up.

Did you know there might be rumors, or market speculation, or more buyers than sellers, or particular sellers, or changes in performance, or volatility, or changes in trading volume, or changing financial projections, or that just generally stocks sometimes go down, including other correlated stocks? That competitors might announce new products, or the public might not like press releases, or there might be public research published that is unfavorable or inaccurate or both? That the float size might change, or new shares might be issued, or new laws passed, or economic conditions might change, or they might be sued, or there might be actual or anticipated changes or fluctuations in the result of Anthropic’s operations?

Now you do.

There Will Be No Dividends

Not for the foreseeable future. You have been warned.

I think this is a mistake. I like the Nvidia strategy of issuing a $0.01 dividend, which allows you to be included in various indexes.

We also learn the stock limits, in case there is ever a fun related Matt Levine column: 300 billion Class A shares, 100 billion Class N shares, 30 billion Class E shares, 30 billion shares of preferred stock and the single Class F and single Class T shares.

What Are We Even Doing?

There might be a war. Terrorism. Natural disaster. Health crisis. Political crisis.

The more I read the risks section, the more I understand what it is doing. This is my first S-1, and this is how you play the game of ‘list everything that could possibly go wrong, one way or another.’

I could go on. I won’t. Around page 90 I started barely skimming the titles. Tax laws could change. ESG disputes could arise. Yeah, yeah. Why are we doing this?

It’s a fun game in some senses, but you would not want to read the results. A Pangram spot check says these sections are a mix of AI and not-AI. If anything I would have used AI more.

This is the perfect case for AI writing. It is text no one needs to write, and text no one needs to read. It is all pro forma, a thing that has to exist so that if anyone asks ‘does this exist?’ the answer comes back yes. It is a gotcha list of gotchas, and we gotcha.

I have been told that, while that might be its purpose, the gotchas are extremely expensive if someone is got, and that lines are gone over one at a time by committees charging $10k an hour that will be some of the last human cognitive jobs on the planet. I get where that rent seeking comes from, and for Anthropic I guess you just pay the bandits, but I don’t see why it changes anything, especially since there is no real penalty that I can see for warning too much about too many things.

The Financial Model

The stock market works on ‘normal’ financial models, so we get a normal financial model. Anthropic invests in compute, uses compute, sells compute and operates.

In some senses I suppose this is a model? It is a very high-level model, I suppose.

Our Financial Model

Our financial model is built on four primary drivers that define the trajectory of our results:

  • Adoption of Claude. The advancing intelligence and capabilities of each successive version of a Claude model drive the diffusion of Claude across the global economy. As new customers adopt Claude and existing customers expand their usage into new workflows, our revenue grows.
  • Compute Efficiency. We are focused on increasing the intelligence produced and revenue generated per dollar of compute invested and have delivered significant efficiency improvements.
  • Operating Efficiency. Our high talent density, efficient go-to-market, and how extensively our teams leverage Claude in their work help to drive improved operating margin, Adjusted Operating Margin, and revenue per employee.
  • Compute Investments. Investing in compute is critical to support our long-term growth, and we intend to continue making substantial investments in compute.

The drivers of our financial model materialize on different timelines.

Claude is sold through all three major cloud platforms (AWS, GCP and Azure) and through various other methods. Growth is what we call ‘gangbusters.’

Our customers with $100k or more of revenue on a TTM basis included every company in the Fortune 10, over 50% of the Fortune 500, and over 30% of the Global 2000.

Within the Fortune 500, these customers included the 10 largest software and IT services companies, the 10 largest internet companies, nine of the 10 largest pharmaceutical companies, the 10 largest banks, nine of the 10 largest semiconductor companies, and eight of the 10 largest healthcare companies. ​

On top of that, existing customers have Net Revenue Retention of ~900%. Which is good, because the above could be called ‘market saturation.’

I suppose that’s one way to Model This.

Next up is compute efficiency, which then breaks down into training efficiency (going up), inference efficiency (going up) and multi-chip compute approach.

Compute is getting increasingly efficiently turned into revenue.

Operating efficiency is up. More is being operated by less people per operation.

Anthropic makes compute investments.

Anthropic then sells Claude inference, including via subscriptions.

They then work with customers, as they integrate Claude into workflows and use more Claude for more of the things over time.

This ‘model’ does not allow you to predict much, other than ‘wow it looks like numbers are going up and getting better, perhaps they will make a lot of money.’

You can tell the model is not that useful since the ‘key factors affecting our performance’ then get repeated from earlier without being directly in the model.

They also repeat a bunch of the financial number statements in adjusted form.

Later, when evaluating the fair value of the common stock pre-IPO, the board of directors ‘exercised reasonable judgment and considered numerous objective and subjective factors,’ including:

  1. Number of future buyers.
  2. Number of future sellers.
  3. Whether there will be more buyers than sellers, or more sellers than buyers.

Oh, sorry, I am informed that instead they claim they looked at other things, but hey.

The Business of Intelligence and Maybe Killing Everyone

There is a lot of repetition in an S-1. The ‘business’ section goes over a lot of the same facts from earlier, that I’ve already gone over.

This is where they get gathered together, and get to emphasize ‘hey did you know Claude is increasingly able to do all the digital things and also interface with the physical things, and it’s going to keep improving and follow the scaling laws?’

If you’re reading this, you already know Claude is going to do all the things, and which products will be used to do that, so this is about how that is being presented to investors. There is no way to properly convey what Claude can do in an S-1, or the true vision of what is coming, especially without worrying about securities fraud if things do not work out so well.

But yeah, It’s Coming. They say what they can for those with eyes to see.

All digital work is ultimately an expression of code, and Claude’s mastery of it powers Virtual Collaborators capable of handling complex work far beyond software development.

… We are building towards a world where Claude can be given open-ended tasks lasting hours, days, or weeks, and then execute them autonomously with the judgment and initiative of a brilliant colleague.

…A core driver of Claude’s diffusion is its intelligence.

…Each new primitive and application we release expands the range of workflows they can run on Claude.

You do have to extrapolate a bit, or you miss most of what is going to be happening.

Otherwise, how many times can you say you will do the various good things? A lot.

They spell out what all their current products are. Claude [Code / Cowork / .ai / Security / Tag / Design / Science]. You’ve got Claude for [Financial Services / Financial Advisors / Healthcare / Life Sciences / Legal / Education / Government]. It’s all Claude.

One new-to-me term was Prosumers, which I think stands for ‘professional consumers’ and means individual Pro or Max subscribers. I’m a prosumer.

They show off and highlight successful partnerships with Accenture, AIG (oh no, is this alphabetical, it looks like it is alphabetical), Bristol Myers Squibb, Doordash, International Rescue Committee, Jane Street, Legora, Lilly, Mercado Libre, Mozilla, PayPal, Rakuten, Salesforce, SAP, Shopify, Travelers, UST, Verizon, Walmart and featuring Shy Bird and KBF.

Different companies offer different stats and use cases. The gains look large for those who do a lot of coding. Coding outputs seem credibly to be +100% or more. For others it is modest, such as PayPal’s 45 minutes saved per sales team member per week. Then again, is ~2% time saved from a custom-built plugin not much, or is it a lot? What about the 25 hours per month saved per consultant at SAP, or ~14%? Over the next year I expect that answer to change.

Don’t Give a Damn About My Regulation

Anthropic reiterates its position, and paints itself as pro-regulation.

We believe that the responsible development of AI requires thoughtful governance, and we actively support efforts by governments and regulatory bodies to establish frameworks that promote safe, beneficial AI. We were founded on the premise that AI systems must be developed with safety and societal benefit as central priorities, and we believe that well-designed regulation can reinforce those values across the industry.

Because AI development at the frontier is a relatively nascent and rapidly evolving field, the laws, regulations, and standards in place today were not necessarily designed with these technologies in mind. We have proactively engaged with legislators, regulators, and other stakeholders in the United States and internationally to promote the development of regulatory frameworks that we believe are good for society, our customers, and the long-term health of the economy, and we intend to continue doing so.

For example, we entered into an agreement with the CAISSI whereby we committed to provide access to our models for testing and evaluation before and after their public release, agreed to provide model access to the U.K. AI Security Institute for pre-deployment testing consistent with our agreement with the CAISSI, and publicly endorsed California’s Transparency in Frontier Artificial Intelligence Act (SB 53).

See recent other posts on Anthropic for my response to that. Anthropic is in some ways performing better than other labs, and they do prioritize the provisions they feel are most important, even when they are not the obvious ones. But I do not feel their proposals are meeting the moment, and this is not a new issue.

This is an S-1, so the actual question here is impact on Anthropic’s bottom line. They don’t have that much to say about that, other than laying out some basic past events.

The Bottom Line

Ultimately, the bottom line is the bottom line. The S-1 is all about what investors care about, and what will guard against being sued for securities fraud or otherwise getting the financial types Big Mad at Anthropic. Other audiences are secondary.

Anthropic remains a frustrating company. Now we know a lot more about it.
